headline: AI App Builders Got the Design Sequence Backwards
lede: A software designer argues that the entire interface paradigm of AI-assisted app creation is structurally wrong. The tools treat a text prompt as the primary creative surface, but design is not a linear conversation — it is a visual, iterative, branching process. The fix, the argument goes, is to invert the sequence entirely.
body:
The category of tools known as *vibe coding* — AI builders where you describe an app in plain language and watch code materialize — have quietly converged on the same user experience: one chat window, one idea at a time, one build per prompt. The implicit model is that language is the best proxy for intent. This argument challenges that assumption at its foundation.

The core claim is structural. When design and code generation are collapsed into a single linear thread, every change in visual direction becomes a fight against existing code rather than a direct manipulation of the design itself. Users end up prompt-engineering their way toward a layout instead of selecting it. The proposed alternative is a **visual-first loop**: flood the screen with AI-generated design options, let the user narrow them down by selecting favorites, lock in a *style system* (a set of reusable design tokens — colors, type scales, spacing rules — that enforces visual consistency across an interface), then auto-scaffold the necessary pages and flows before compiling code once as the terminal step.

The logic is tighter than it initially appears. AI can now generate dozens of visual variants in seconds at negligible cost, which eliminates the old practical argument for skipping early-stage visual exploration: that it takes too long. If exploration is cheap and fast, the correct interface surfaces many options simultaneously rather than generating them one at a time through description.

The argument resonates most for the actual workload of AI builders — landing pages, marketing sites, dashboards, early-stage prototypes — where the visual outcome *is* the product. It is a harder case to make for applications with complex state, business logic, or backend dependencies, where design and code have always needed to evolve together rather than in strict sequence. The author does not fully engage with this boundary.

Two tools are named as partial examples of the right approach: *Relume* and *Magic Path AI*. No research sources were available to assess their current capabilities in detail, and the author hedges appropriately, saying only that they are "on the right track" rather than claiming either has solved the problem end to end.

concepts.definition: A term for AI-assisted software development in which a user describes desired functionality in natural language and an AI generates the corresponding code. Coined by researcher Andrej Karpathy, it has come to describe a broad category of tools where the emphasis is on speed and accessibility over deep technical knowledge.

A structured set of reusable design decisions — color palettes, typography scales, spacing units, component patterns — that enforces visual consistency across a product. Analogous to a house style in publishing: once defined, every new element is derived from it rather than invented from scratch.

A design process in which visual output is produced and evaluated before any code is written. The designer explores options at the layout and aesthetic level, selects a direction, and only then hands off to implementation. Contrasts with prompt-driven workflows where code generation precedes visual review.
